sources.title: Performance Hints — Jeff Dean & Sanjay Ghemawat (abseil Performance Guide)
abseil / Performance Guide (the series this document belongs to)

structure.rationale: The book follows the source document's own spine, because that spine is itself the argument: you cannot optimize what you cannot estimate, you should not optimize what you have not measured, and once you are measuring, the wins arrive in a predictable order of leverage — interface shape, then algorithm, then memory representation, then allocation count, then work avoided outright. Each chapter is one of the document's top-level sections, kept in its original order so a reader can hold the book beside the original. 'Make the compiler's job easier' stays inside the final chapter, as it is a subsection of 'Avoid unnecessary work' in the source rather than a peer of it.
structure.audience: Working programmers who write code that other code depends on — library authors, systems and backend engineers. Examples are C++ because the source document is C++, but every principle here is about memory, cache lines and counted work, so it reads across languages.

claims.text: The document was written by Jeff Dean and Sanjay Ghemawat as an internal Google document and later published externally as part of the abseil Performance Guide.

Knuth's 'premature optimization is the root of all evil' is routinely quoted without its surrounding sentence, which says to forget small efficiencies about 97% of the time while not passing up the opportunities in the critical 3%.
Hoare/Knuth's own framing includes the observation that 'a 12% improvement, easily obtained, is never considered marginal' in other engineering disciplines.
Deferring all performance thinking tends to produce a flat profile: the cost is spread so thinly that no single hot spot appears to attack.

Three costs of deferring performance work: diffuse problems are harder to locate and fix; users of a library usually cannot make the improvement themselves; and a system already in heavy use is difficult to change retroactively.
The document's recommended posture while writing code is to choose the faster alternative when it does not significantly impact the readability or complexity of the code.

pitfalls: Reading the advice as licence to micro-optimize everything: the document explicitly ties effort to whether code is on a hot path, in initialization, or in a widely-used library.
Reading it as licence to defer everything: that is the flat-profile trap the chapter is about.

claims.text: Before measuring, estimate: the document argues for building intuition about the cost of operations so a design can be judged on paper.

The document's reference cost table gives: L1 cache reference 0.5 ns; L2 cache reference 3 ns; branch mispredict 5 ns; uncontended mutex lock/unlock 15 ns; main memory reference 50 ns; compress 1K bytes with Snappy 1,000 ns; read 4KB from SSD 20,000 ns; round trip within the same datacenter 50,000 ns; read 1MB sequentially from memory 64,000 ns; read 1MB over a 100 Gbps network 100,000 ns; read 1MB from SSD 1,000,000 ns; disk seek 5,000,000 ns; read 1MB sequentially from disk 10,000,000 ns; send a packet CA->Netherlands->CA 150,000,000 ns.

Worked example — quicksorting one billion 4-byte numbers: roughly 30 passes over 4GB, memory transfer about 0.25s per pass giving about 7.5 seconds, plus roughly 15 billion branch mispredictions at 5 ns each giving about 75 seconds, for an estimate near 82.5 seconds.

Worked example — building a web page with 30 thumbnails: reading the images serially at about 15 ms each costs about 450 ms; reading them in parallel across many disks brings latency to about 15 ms; serving from SSD costs about 30 ms.
Where code sits determines how much estimation effort it deserves: initialization code, hot-path code, and library code used by many applications carry very different budgets.

pitfalls: Treating the table's numbers as exact for a specific machine — they are order-of-magnitude anchors for arithmetic, and the absolute values drift with hardware generations.
Estimating only the obvious cost (bytes moved) and forgetting the second term (branch mispredicts, round trips), which in the quicksort example is ten times larger.

claims.text: The document recommends reaching for pprof first, because it gives good high-level performance information and is easy to use both locally and against code running in production.
Build production binaries with appropriate debugging information so profiles are attributable to source.
Write microbenchmarks for the code being improved, and use a benchmark library that can emit hardware performance-counter readings.
Lock contention can artificially lower measured CPU usage, so a CPU profile alone can hide a contention problem.

When a profile is flat, the document's suggested moves are: accumulate many 1% improvements across a subsystem; look for loops near the top of call stacks as candidates for restructuring; seek structural rather than micro changes; replace over-general code with specialized implementations; use allocation profiling to reduce allocation counts; and gather hardware counters to find cache misses.

pitfalls: Concluding from a flat profile that there is nothing to win — a flat profile is a symptom of diffuse cost, not of an optimal program.
Profiling a binary built without debug information, then attributing time to the wrong frames.

claims.text: Bulk APIs reduce the number of expensive API-boundary crossings and can enable algorithmic improvements that a one-at-a-time interface forecloses.
A bulk deletion API such as ObjectStore::DeleteRefs amortizes locking overhead by acquiring the mutex once for many operations instead of once per operation.
A bulk lookup interface can also simplify the return type — for example when clients only need to know whether all keys were found.
When converting callers to a bulk API is difficult, a type can use bulk operations internally and cache the results to serve future non-bulk calls.
The document advises preferring view types for function arguments — std::string_view, absl::Span<T>, absl::FunctionRef<R(Args...)> — to reduce copying and let callers choose their own container.
Accepting a pre-computed argument (for example a WallTime the caller already has) avoids recomputing it inside the callee.

Most types should be thread-compatible (externally synchronized) rather than thread-safe, so callers that do not need synchronization do not pay for it; when synchronization is nearly always needed, moving it inside the type allows internal optimization without changing callers.

snippets.note: One mutex acquisition for the whole batch instead of one per reference.

snippets.code:
static void RecordRPC(const Name &name, const RPC_Stats_Measurement& m,
                      WallTime now);
snippets.note: The caller passes the clock reading it already has, so the callee does not read the clock again.
The lock was removed once callers were known to be externally synchronized.

pitfalls: Adding a bulk API but leaving every caller on the singular one, so the boundary crossings never actually go away.
Making a type thread-safe by default and thereby taxing every single-threaded caller.

claims.text: Algorithmic improvements are the highest-leverage category: turning O(N^2) into O(N log N) or O(N), or removing exponential behaviour entirely.
GraphCycles was changed from adding nodes and edges incrementally to adding the whole graph in reverse post-order, which makes cycle detection a rank comparison as edges are added.
An IntervalMap with O(log N) lookups was replaced by a hash table with O(1) lookups once adjacent-block discovery could be done by lookup rather than by traversal.
Intersecting two sorted lists at O(N log N) was replaced by hashing one side and probing it with the other, at O(N).
A hash table only delivers O(1) behaviour if its hash function actually spreads the keys; a poor hash function degrades lookups toward O(N).

snippets.note: Building the whole graph at once turns incremental cycle maintenance into one DFS plus a rank comparison per edge.

pitfalls: Micro-optimizing the inner loop of an algorithm that should have been replaced.
Assuming a hash container is O(1) without checking the hash function on the actual key distribution.

claims.text: A compact representation reduces memory usage and improves performance by touching fewer cache lines and using less memory-bus bandwidth; it is most worth doing for data accessed often or making up a large share of the application's memory.
Compaction has a counter-indication: packing separately-written data together can create cache-line contention between threads.
Reordering fields to group equal alignment requirements minimizes padding inside a type.
Using a smaller numeric type when the range allows it, such as uint8_t instead of int, shrinks the type.
Giving an enum an explicit underlying type — enum class OpType : uint8_t — makes its storage size explicit rather than defaulting to int width.
Placing frequently-accessed fields next to each other reduces the number of cache lines touched by a common operation.
Separating hot read-only fields from hot mutable fields keeps writes from evicting shared read-only data.
Cold data should be moved to the end of the struct, behind an indirection, or into a separate array.
Bit- and byte-level encodings can cut memory substantially but should live behind a well-tested encapsulation boundary and be justified by benchmarks.
On a 64-bit machine a pointer costs 64 bits; an index into an array can often be 32 bits or fewer, and storing elements contiguously also improves cache locality.

snippets.code: enum class OpType : uint8_t { kAdd, kMul, kLoad, kStore };
snippets.note: An explicit underlying type; without it the enum is int-width.

pitfalls: Packing fields that different threads write, turning a size win into false sharing.
Hand-rolling a bit encoding without an encapsulation boundary, so every future reader has to understand it.

claims.text: Containers that allocate a separate node per element, such as std::map and std::unordered_map, have worse cache behaviour and more allocator overhead than flat or chunked containers such as std::vector and absl::flat_hash_map/flat_hash_set.
Partitioning elements into fixed-size chunks reduces the cache footprint while keeping good asymptotic complexity.

Inlined containers such as InlinedVector embed space for a small number of elements and avoid allocating at all when the count stays small; this pays off when instances are stack variables or exist in large numbers.
Inlined storage is a poor fit when sizeof(T) is large, because the embedded backing store then makes every instance large.

A nested map btree<a, btree<b, c>> can often be flattened to btree<pair<a,b>, c>, cutting lookup and insertion cost; the document's example flattens absl::btree_map<std::string, absl::btree_map<std::string, OpDef>> to absl::btree_map<std::pair<absl::string_view, absl::string_view>, const OpDef*>.
Flattening is not always right: if the first key is large, the nested form may be better because the key is stored once.

Arenas reduce allocation cost, pack independently-allocated items into fewer cache lines, and remove destruction overhead; they suit complex structures with many sub-objects and should be given a sensible initial size.
Arenas have a counter-indication: putting many short-lived objects in a long-lived arena bloats memory.

When a map's domain is small integers or an enum, or holds very few elements, a plain array or vector usually beats a map — one example replaced const gtl::flat_map<int, int> payload_type_to_clock_frequency_ with int map[128].

When a set's domain is small integers, a bit vector replaces a hash set, with OR for union and AND for intersection; replacing dense_hash_set<ZoneId> with util::bitmap::InlinedBitVector<256> gave 26-31% improvements across benchmarks.

snippets.note: The flattened form also drops to string_view keys and a pointer value.
Direct indexing removes hashing, probing and node allocation together.

pitfalls: Reaching for a hash map by reflex when the key domain is a small dense integer range.
Putting short-lived objects into a long-lived arena and turning an allocation win into a memory leak in all but name.

claims.text: An allocation costs three things: time inside the allocator, any expensive initialization and destruction of the object, and a larger cache footprint because each allocation usually lands on a fresh cache line.
Caching a shared pointer to a single empty DeviceInfo instead of constructing a new one increased benchmark throughput by 21%.
Using a statically-allocated zero vector where possible avoids allocating a vector and filling it with zeroes.
Pre-sizing a container and filling it directly avoids the repeated reallocation of N push_back calls.
The document cautions against using resize or reserve to grow one element at a time, which can produce quadratic behaviour.

Preferring moves to copies, and storing pointers or indices rather than object copies, removes copying overhead; eliminating one extra copy in a benchmark sending roughly 400KB tensors over gRPC gave about a 10-15% speedup.

Hoisting a container or message declaration outside a loop and clearing it between iterations reuses one buffer instead of allocating per iteration; serializing repeatedly into a caller-supplied scratch string is the same idea across an API boundary.

snippets.note: One shared empty instance; the 21% throughput win in the document.
The document's hoist-and-Clear pattern for a protobuf inside a loop.

pitfalls: Calling reserve inside the loop it is meant to hoist out of, which reintroduces quadratic growth.
Counting only allocator time and ignoring the cache-footprint cost, which is often the larger of the two.

claims.text: A fast path handles the common case cheaply and falls back to the general code otherwise; the document's examples include UTF-8 scanning that handles trailing single ASCII bytes separately, a simplified InlinedVector resize, fast paths for 1-D to 4-D tensor shape initialization, and a varint parser whose inlined fast path covers only the 1-byte case.
Keeping the inlined fast path small reduces code size and instruction-cache pressure.
Guarding a loop behind a flag that says whether any work is needed skips the loop entirely in the common case.

Precomputing a property once at initialization — for example whether a node is an Enter or Exit node — turns a repeated test into a flag check; computing a probability lookup table once rather than inside an inner loop is the same move.
Hoisting a bounds computation, or any loop-invariant expression, out of the loop body avoids recomputing it every iteration.
Deferring GetSubSharding() calls until they were actually needed reduced 43 seconds of CPU time to 2 seconds.
Computing statistics on demand in a Stats() call, instead of updating them eagerly on every allocation and deallocation, moves the cost off the hot path.
Reducing pre-allocated initial query nodes from 200 to 10 cut CPU usage by 7.5%.

Specialized code can beat a general library: a custom histogram printer was about 4x as fast as sprintf, RE2 calls were replaced by simple prefix matching where a full regex was not needed, and StrCat replaced StringPrintf for formatting IP addresses.
Caching a result keyed on a precomputed fingerprint avoids re-parsing a large serialized proto on every access.
Compilers must assume conservatively across abstraction boundaries, so a programmer who knows more about the actual behaviour can help — but only after profiling identifies the bottleneck.

Ways to help the compiler: eliminate function calls on hot paths to avoid frame setup, move slow-path code into tail-called functions, copy data into local variables before heavy use so the compiler can discard aliasing assumptions and auto-vectorize, and hand-unroll very hot loops.

Concrete compiler-assist examples in the document: replacing absl::Span with raw pointers to the underlying arrays in ForEachState; hand-unrolling a CRC loop to process 16 bytes per iteration instead of 4; and parsing a key four characters at a time, scanning backwards for the separator instead of calling memchr.

snippets.note: One flag test replaces NUM_ERRORS additions in the overwhelmingly common no-error case.

pitfalls: Growing a fast path until it is no longer fast: the document's varint example deliberately covers only the 1-byte case to keep the inlined code small.
Helping the compiler before profiling, which trades readability for nothing.
Deferring a computation that then happens twice, so the deferral costs more than it saves.

volatile: The latency reference numbers — they are order-of-magnitude anchors and drift with hardware generations
